content:
The circulatory system is a vital biological transport network that delivers oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and immune cells throughout the body while removing waste products like carbon dioxide. At the center of this system is the heart, a muscular organ that functions as a powerful pump, contracting and relaxing to create the pressure needed to move blood through approximately 60,000 miles of blood vessels in an adult human body.
 Blood circulation follows a specific pathway known as the double circulation system, consisting of two primary loops: the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit. In the pulmonary circuit, deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle of the heart through the pulmonary artery and travels to the lungs, where it releases carbon dioxide and absorbs oxygen. The now-oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium of the heart through the pulmonary veins. In the systemic circuit, this oxygen-rich blood is pumped from the left ventricle through the aorta and distributed to tissues throughout the body via progressively smaller arteries and arterioles. After oxygen and nutrients are exchanged at the capillary level, the deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium through venules and veins, particularly the superior and inferior venae cavae.
 The one-way flow of blood is maintained through a series of valves that prevent backflow. The heart contains two sets of valves: atrioventricular valves (the tricuspid between the right atrium and ventricle, and the mitral between the left atrium and ventricle) and semilunar valves (the pulmonary valve at the exit of the right ventricle and the aortic valve at the exit of the left ventricle). Veins also contain small valves that ensure blood flows only toward the heart, which is especially important in the legs where blood must fight against gravity.
 Blood vessels are specialized structures with different functions in the circulatory system. Arteries have thick, elastic walls to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart, while veins have thinner walls but larger lumens and valves to facilitate the lower-pressure return of blood to the heart. Capillaries, with their single-cell-thick walls, form the interface between the circulatory system and tissues, allowing for the efficient exchange of substances through diffusion, active transport, and bulk flow processes.

scenario.title: Hallway Highways: Blood Circulation Simulator
scenario.content: In this simulation, students navigate a virtual school building where hallways represent blood vessels and students represent blood cells. The simulation enforces one-way traffic patterns with designated paths for oxygenated and deoxygenated 'students,' mimicking arteries and veins. Bottlenecks occur when traffic rules are violated, demonstrating how proper circulatory pathways prevent congestion. Students explore concepts like the cardiac cycle, valve function, and various circulatory problems through scenarios that require proper routing and flow management.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Understanding Directional Flow in Circulatory Systems
hypothesis.description: Students will be able to describe the one-way flow pattern of blood through the cardiovascular system, identify the major blood vessels and heart chambers involved in pulmonary and systemic circulation, and explain how valves and vessel specialization maintain efficient unidirectional flow.
